old: The gentleman seemed to experience some change of feeling
new: The gentleman experienced some change of feeling
source: The gentleman experienced some change of feeling
reason: The narrator states the change as fact; the candidate adds a hedge ('seemed to'), weakening the narrator's direct report of Darcy's feeling.

old: It seemed like deliberate bad luck or voluntary penance
new: It seemed like deliberate spite, or a voluntary penance
source: It seemed like wilful ill-nature, or a voluntary penance
reason: 'Ill-nature' means malice, not luck; Elizabeth's joke is that Darcy seems to be doing it on purpose, either to spite her or to punish himself. 'Deliberate bad luck' makes no sense.

old: how deeply I admire and love you
new: how ardently I admire and love you
source: how ardently I admire and love you
reason: 'Ardently' is still plain modern English and gives the passion of Darcy's famous declaration; 'deeply' flattens it.

old: and if I _could_ feel grateful, I would now thank you
new: and if I could _feel_ gratitude, I would now thank you
source: and if I could _feel_ gratitude, I would now thank you
reason: Austen stresses _feel_, contrasting actually feeling gratitude with the 'established mode' of expressing it. Moving the stress to _could_ changes the point.

old: Elizabeth refused to dignify this self-serving remark with a response
new: Elizabeth disdained even to appear to notice this civil remark
source: Elizabeth disdained the appearance of noticing this civil reflection
reason: 'Civil reflection' is ironic: the remark is polite in form and insulting in meaning. 'Self-serving' replaces the irony with a flat judgment, and 'refused to dignify it with a response' is a modern cliché.
lead_note: Defect accepted; "scorned to show" is an archaic construction, so this keeps the source verb (disdained) in a modern pattern.

old: But dishonesty of every kind is hateful to me.
new: But disguise of every kind is hateful to me.
source: But disguise of every sort is my abhorrence.
reason: Darcy means concealing his feelings, not lying. 'Disguise' also sets up his admission in the letter (35.4, 'this concealment, this disguise, was beneath me'), and 'dishonesty' breaks that link.

old: built such an unshakeable dislike that I had not known you a month before
new: built so unshakeable a dislike; and I had not known you a month before
source: on which succeeding events have built so immovable a dislike; and I had not known you a month before I felt
reason: The candidate's 'such... that' makes the one-month verdict a result of the later events. In the source these are two separate claims joined by 'and', and within a month comes before the 'succeeding events'.

old: whose cruel treatment he had not even tried to deny
new: his cruelty toward whom he had not even tried to deny
source: his cruelty towards whom he had not attempted to deny
reason: 'Whose cruel treatment' can be read as Wickham's cruelty. The source means Darcy's cruelty toward Wickham.

old: forgive the liberty I take in asking for your attention; your feelings, I know, will give it reluctantly, but I ask it in the name of fairness.
new: forgive the freedom with which I demand your attention; your feelings, I know, will give it reluctantly, but I demand it of your sense of justice.
source: You must, therefore, pardon the freedom with which I demand your attention; your feelings, I know, will bestow it unwillingly, but I demand it of your justice.
reason: Darcy 'demands' twice. Changing this to 'asking' softens his haughty stiffness at the start of the letter, which Elizabeth then reacts to ('his style was not penitent, but haughty').

old: That I _wanted_ to believe her indifferent is certain
new: That I wanted to believe her indifferent is certain
source: That I was desirous of believing her indifferent is certain
reason: The emphasis on 'wanted' is not in the source and adds a stress that Darcy's even admission does not have.

old: though not ideal, was nothing compared
new: though objectionable, was nothing compared
source: The situation of your mother's family, though objectionable, was nothing in comparison
reason: 'Not ideal' is a modern softener that makes Darcy more tactful than he is. The source says 'objectionable'.

old: was hardly the work of a moment
new: took scarcely a moment
source: was scarcely the work of a moment
reason: Today 'hardly the work of a moment' reads as 'took real effort', which reverses the meaning. Darcy means that persuading Bingley was almost instant.

old: Perhaps this concealment was beneath me.
new: Perhaps this concealment, this disguise, was beneath me.
source: Perhaps this concealment, this disguise, was beneath me.
reason: This drops 'this disguise', Darcy's own word from the proposal scene ('disguise of every sort is my abhorrence'). Here he admits to the very thing he claimed to abhor.

old: The regret he expressed for what he'd done didn't satisfy her;
new: He expressed no regret for what he had done that satisfied her;
source: He expressed no regret for what he had done which satisfied her
reason: The candidate says outright that Darcy expressed regret. The source only says that no regret he expressed satisfied her, and leaves open whether he expressed any.

old: What Wickham had said about the living
new: What Wickham had said about the parish
source: What Wickham had said of the living
reason: The edition calls the 'living' a 'parish' everywhere else, including the letter just before (35.4) and Wickham's account (16.23-27). 'The living' here reads as a new, unexplained term.

old: Wickham's giving up all claim to the living
new: Wickham's giving up all claim to the parish
source: of Wickham's resigning all pretensions to the living
reason: This keeps the term consistent with the letter's 'parish', as in the previous proposal.

old: she flattered herself that her own judgment wasn't wrong
new: she flattered herself that her wishes weren't wrong
source: she flattered herself that her wishes did not err
reason: The irony is that she trusts her wishes (to believe Wickham), not her judgment. Saying 'judgment' removes the self-deception the chapter goes on to expose.

old: But the story that followed, of his designs
new: But, alas, the story that followed, of his designs
source: But, alas! the story which followed, of his designs on Miss Darcy
reason: This drops the narrator's 'alas!', which gives Elizabeth's rueful reluctance at a key turn.

old: to prove him capable of genuine feeling
new: to prove him capable of some kindly feeling
source: as to prove him capable of some amiable feeling
reason: The candidate drops Elizabeth's grudging 'some' and the kind of feeling ('amiable'), which inflates what she concedes.

old: the contempt their behavior had brought upon the rest of her family
new: the contempt the rest of her family had thus brought upon themselves
source: the contempt which had been thus self-attracted by the rest of her family
reason: 'Their behavior' can be read as the behavior of Elizabeth and Jane, the subject of the previous clause. The source says the rest of the family drew the contempt on themselves.

old: a compliment and a subtle reference to offer here
new: a compliment and an allusion to offer here
source: Mr. Collins had a compliment and an allusion to throw in here
reason: 'Subtle' is invented, and it goes against the comedy of Mr. Collins, who is never subtle.

old: traveling by post alone
new: traveling alone in hired carriages
source: two young women travelling post by themselves
reason: 'By post' now suggests the mail. Traveling post meant traveling in hired carriages with horses changed at inns, which is what Lady Catherine objects to without a servant.
lead_note: Defect accepted; the proposed wording was awkward. This keeps the meaning of traveling post (hired carriages, no servant) without the misleading "by post".

old: it would really be a discredit to you to let them go alone
new: it would really be a discredit to _you_ to let them go alone
source: it would really be discreditable to _you_ to let them go alone
reason: The candidate drops Austen's emphasis. Lady Catherine pointedly turns the impropriety into Charlotte's own discredit.

old: the entrance of the lady who was its subject
new: the entrance of the lady from whom those comforts sprang
source: the entrance of the lady from whom they sprang
reason: The irony is that Charlotte is the source of Mr. Collins's domestic comforts. 'Its subject' loses that and makes the referent vague.

old: must at the same time gratify whatever
new: must at the same time so highly gratify whatever
source: must, at the same time, so highly gratify whatever of her own vanity
reason: This drops the degree ('so highly'), which weakens the admitted pull of Elizabeth's vanity, the temptation the sentence is about.
